articles.title: How Cursor’s Agent Mode Works and How to Host Its Claude Tool on ECS Fargate, Explained Simply
articles.excerpt: Cursor turns your editor into an AI‑native workspace, but the heavy LLM calls can still slow you down. By offloading the Claude‑powered tool server to ECS Fargate you keep the IDE snappy while gaining…
articles.body: Cursor turns your editor into an AI‑native workspace, but the heavy LLM calls can still slow you down. By offloading the Claude‑powered tool server to ECS Fargate you keep the IDE snappy while gaining unlimited scalability. This post shows exactly how to wire the two together. Understanding Cursor’s Agent Mode What is Agent Mode? Cursor ships with a built‑in LLM (large language model) that can suggest code, refactor, or answer questions. When it needs to do something it can’t do locally—like running a test suite, reading a remote file, or calling a cloud service—it switches to Agent Mode . In this mode Cursor sends a tool call (an HTTP request) to a tiny web server you provide.

articles.title: What ABA 509 Disclosures Actually Tell You About Law School Admissions
articles.excerpt: If you are comparing US law schools, the single most useful public dataset is the ABA 509 disclosure. Every ABA-accredited school publishes one each year, and it contains the numbers that actually mat…
articles.body: If you are comparing US law schools, the single most useful public dataset is the ABA 509 disclosure. Every ABA-accredited school publishes one each year, and it contains the numbers that actually matter for admissions: acceptance rate, the median LSAT and GPA of the entering class, and the 25th/75th percentiles behind those medians. Why the 509 is worth reading Most ranking systems mix in reputation surveys or outcome data that are hard to reproduce. The 509 is different: the figures are reported by the schools themselves to the ABA, so you can verify them at the source. A few things I always look at: Median vs. 25th/75th percentiles. The median LSAT tells you the midpoint, not the floor. If your score sits below the 25th percentile, the median alone gives a false sense of fit.

articles.title: Optimistic HTTP upgrades need a rule for bytes sent before confirmation
articles.excerpt: Optimistic HTTP upgrades need a rule for bytes sent before confirmation HTTP/1.1 can ask to change the protocol on an existing connection. A client that sends data before the server confirms the trans…
articles.body: Optimistic HTTP upgrades need a rule for bytes sent before confirmation HTTP/1.1 can ask to change the protocol on an existing connection. A client that sends data before the server confirms the transition can create a parsing problem for intermediaries and for the application that eventually receives the bytes. RFC 9931 treats that timing as a security issue, especially when a third party controls the request data or the post-transition content. The new standard updates the HTTP/1.1 and UDP-proxying specifications. It discusses transitions such as WebSocket and connect-udp , where the client may begin a new protocol after an upgrade request. The document notes that when only the client and server are involved, each already has to handle arbitrary bytes from the other.

articles.title: 20 Years Later, the PS3’s Biggest Failures Look Like Its Best Ideas
articles.excerpt: Sony's PlayStation 3 was a technological fever dream that fused three consoles, a Blu-ray player, and a supercomputer into one absurd box.
articles.body: It’s fascinating now to think what a total gamble the PS3 was at the time of its release. Even after all these years, there’s no doubt in my mind it’s one of the greatest (and craziest) inventions the video game industry ever came up with. Nowadays, it’s lauded as the most ridiculous, expensive, and over-engineered console ever made. Yet when looking back at Sony circa 2001, just months after the PS2 launched and began its march to becoming the best-selling console of all time (a feat it still holds today), what was Sony supposed to do to top that? Make the PlayStation 3 do literally everything.

articles.title: Satellites now outnumber the visible stars above most towns
articles.excerpt: More than 700 satellites are crossing the sky over an average mid-latitude town at any moment of the night, outnumbering in many cases the stars visible to the naked eye.
articles.body: More than 700 satellites are crossing the sky over an average mid-latitude town at any moment of the night, outnumbering in many cases the stars visible to the naked eye. That's based on an analysis of the trajectories of the 15,833 active satellites that currently circle the planet in low Earth orbit below an altitude of 1,200 miles (2,000 kilometers). Analyzing data from Oct. 12 and 18 this year, researchers found that with a completely unobstructed horizon, 710 satellites were crossing the sky in every single moment of the night above an average U.K. town. The results were published as a non-peer-reviewed study conducted by engineering firm Accu Components, and is based on satellite monitoring data from the U.S. Space Force available through the public website CelesTrak.

articles.excerpt: Time to go on a nostalgia trip.
articles.body: TL;DR Android Time Machine is a website that simulates old versions of Android right in your browser. It currently has eight releases, from Android 2.1 Eclair to Android 7.1.2 Nougat. Each version runs on the Nexus phone it originally shipped on, and there’s nothing to install. Android is by far the most popular mobile operating system out there. However, the Android we see today is very different from what it was years ago, back when Google still named it after desserts (and not just codenames, either) and things like Material 3 Expressive weren’t even on the radar. If you’ve ever wondered what Android was like before gesture navigation, expandable notifications, or even an on-screen back button, a new website could scratch that itch.

articles.body: California is suing OpenAI after its AI agents broke out of their testing environment and hacked other companies, including Hugging Face.
